rows.reachability_reason: The rule `todo` is on by default and copies up to 30 characters of comment text after TODO/FIXME into the reason. swiftc accepts C0 controls inside comments (it rejects them only in literals), so code that compiles and lints cleanly otherwise reaches the bug. A pasted ANSI escape is one way. User-written custom_rules `message` strings (for example colour escapes) reach it too. File paths with control characters reach the escaped `name` attribute the same way. Reproduced end to end with the shipping 0.65.1 binary.

rows.witness:
The judges' exact input, Writer().serializePlist(.string("\u{1}")), run on the census revision's text, returns `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist ...>
<plist version="1.0">
<string>\u{1}</string>
</plist>
`, with U+0001 written raw. Through the public API: PropertyListEncoder with outputFormat = .xml, encoding ["key": "\u{1}"], gives `<dict>
	<key>key</key>
	<string>\u{1}</string>
</dict>`. Dictionary keys go through appendEscaped too, so ["k\u{1}": "v"] gives `<key>k\u{1}</key>`. A Codable struct with a String field set to "\u{1B}[0m" also gives malformed output. The top-level form is refused by encode(_:), but encode(_:configuration:) returns the judges' exact bytes. A sweep of U+0000 to U+0020 plus U+007F, U+0085, U+FFFD, U+FFFE, U+FFFF and U+1FFFE through the shipping encoder found: U+0000 throws (the guard); XMLParser rejects 30 outputs, namely U+0001 to U+0008, U+000B, U+000C, U+000E to U+001F, U+FFFE and U+FFFF; it accepts tab, LF, CR, U+0020, U+007F, U+0085, U+FFFD and U+1FFFE. That is exactly the set XML 1.0's Char production forbids, less the guarded NUL. Controls for comparison: `a<b&c` is escaped as `a<b&c` and parses.

rows.contract_reason: Any Swift String is a legal property-list string value. The binary format writes it, and PropertyListDecoder reads the XML output back unchanged (the round trip returned true). PropertyListEncoder.encode documents only non-conforming floats and errors thrown by values as failures. The writer's one guard is the NUL sentinel, which throws CocoaError .propertyListWriteInvalid and is excluded by the law. That guard came from swift-foundation PR #2039, whose stated rationale is 'The XML spec explicitly forbids NUL bytes'. The same spec forbids the other 29 C0 controls and U+FFFE/U+FFFF, and nothing guards those. The reader's own TODO in XMLPlistScanner.parseCDSect_pl at the census revision says control characters are 'supposed to be rejected'. The judges' top-level .string form is refused by encode(_:) (the fragment check at PlistEncoder.swift 155-170), but encode(_:configuration:) at lines 205-209 has no such check and admits it.
rows.reachability_reason: Any app that calls PropertyListEncoder with the .xml format on a Codable String it does not control produces malformed XML: a label a user types, a pasted string carrying ESC, VT or FF, a file name, or text carrying U+FFFF. This was shown with a plain Codable struct (Settings(windowTitle: "\u{1B}]0;x\u{7}")) and with a [String: String] dictionary, including a dictionary key. No precondition or validation sits between Codable input and appendEscaped other than the NUL check. Apple's own reader accepts the output, which hides the defect inside the ecosystem. Any standard XML consumer (XMLParser/libxml2) rejects it.

Related: PR #2039 (merged 2026-06-15, kperryua) added the NUL rejection only, and declined to change deserialization. #2239 (open) is a generic third-party benchmark compliance report that links a dashboard and names no specific case. A search for control characters, invalid characters or escaping in XML plists found no issue or PR.
rows.summary: The witness holds. Run on the census text verbatim and through the shipping macOS PropertyListEncoder, Writer.serializePlist writes any XML-forbidden character other than NUL raw: U+0001-U+0008, U+000B, U+000C, U+000E-U+001F, U+FFFE and U+FFFF, 30 code points in all, in <string> and <key> alike. XMLParser rejects the output with invalidCharacterError (code 9; final parserError 111). The input is an ordinary Codable String and upstream main is unchanged, so this is a reachable defect and a natural follow-up to PR #2039, whose stated rationale (the XML spec forbids the character) covers these code points too. One caveat for the report: XML 1.0 cannot escape these characters, so the only fix is to throw as for NUL, which changes behaviour for callers who now round-trip such strings through PropertyListDecoder.

rows.contract_reason: svg(_:) is public, has no precondition, and takes any RenderScene. RenderScene.Text.string is any String: its doc only says a lowered scene holds no line break, and the type is Codable so that scenes can cross process boundaries. The enum's doc promises a standalone document 'any browser or vector tool can open'. escape's doc says it works 'so labels can't break the doc', and the body breaks that on both inputs. There is no guard sentinel. The parser's own `referenced(_:)` refuses control characters and noncharacters because 'SVG can't hold them', which shows the authors consider such output out of contract. They guarded only one route in.
rows.reachability_reason: Users type Mermaid source, and it reaches the unit through MermaidRenderer.svg(source:theme:), the README's documented SVG export. I reproduced this end to end with ASCII-only source. A flowchart label `"a <́ b"` (or `&́`) has its numeric reference decoded by MermaidParser.labelText to U+0301, which lands right after '<' or '&'. That makes a single grapheme cluster, which escape passes raw. Raw C0 controls (ESC or backspace pasted into a quoted flowchart label, or U+0001 in a sequence message) also pass straight through. The parser blocks only the `` reference route. VT and FF are split into lines, so they do not reach the unit, and pie labels do not decode references.

rows.summary: Confirmed by running it. SVGRenderer.escape works on whole Characters and only swaps the five predefined entities. So C0 controls and noncharacters such as U+FFFE pass into <text> raw, and a '<' or '&' followed by a combining mark is a different Character and passes unescaped. XMLParser rejects all of these, against the doc's claim that labels can't break the doc. The input is reachable from plain ASCII Mermaid source (`A["a <́ b"]`) through the public parse → scene → SVG pipeline, and the defect is unchanged on the default branch.

No parser, preprocessor or TextMeasure.splitHardLines step rejects or strips C0 controls other than \n and \r. No guard returns a sentinel. The README and spec name svgString() as the HTML/PDF export path and promise byte-stable SVG.

rows.reachability_reason: SotoXML is not a library product. SotoCore imports it `internal`. A gh code search finds it imported outside soto-core's Sources only by soto-core's own tests and benchmark and by soto's IntegrationTests. Inside the package, attribute nodes come only from Element.parse. XMLEncoder never creates attributes or comments, and nothing sets version or characterEncoding. Document.xmlString has two production call sites. AWSHTTPRequest (.restxml) writes encoder output plus a constant model xmlns. S3Middleware.getBucketLocationResponseFixup re-serialises a parsed S3 LocationConstraint whose only attribute is the xmlns URI, and a comment parsed from well-formed XML cannot hold "--". The parse-then-re-serialise break therefore needs an S3 endpoint that sends an escaped character in an attribute on LocationConstraint. A separate Law-1 failure is reachable: a user string holding a character XML 1.0 forbids (U+0001, U+FFFE), for example an S3 DeleteObjects key or a tag value, passes through xmlEncode raw. XML 1.0 cannot carry such a character even as a character reference, so AWS rejects the body whatever soto does, and the only loss is a clear client-side error.
rows.upstream_note: The default branch is main, and its HEAD is the census revision itself (ec2b3a73, committed 2026-10-20). rows.summary: Document.xmlString writes attribute values, namespace values, version, encoding and comment text without escaping. The judges' witness gives `<r k="&"></r>`, which XMLParser rejects (68, xmlParseEntityRef: no name), and version `1"0` and comment `a--b` also fail. The attribute case is a real departure from the Foundation classes the file says it mirrors, and it breaks parse-then-re-serialise of `k="a&b"`. But SotoXML is internal to SotoCore, and no production caller creates attributes, comments or a version, so it is mention-only. The only reachable Law-1 failure, a forbidden control character in a request string, is one AWS would reject anyway.
